segments.english: "Look, please, I have two daughters who have never known a man. Let me bring them out to you now, and do to them as you see fit. Only, to these men do not do anything, since they have come under the shelter of my roof."
segments.literal: look-please to-me two-of daughters who not knew man let-me-bring-out now them to-you and-do to-them as-the-good in-eyes-of-you only to-the-men these not do a-thing for-on-account-of-this came in-shadow-of roof-of-me

tokens.note: הִנֵּה calls attention: 'look', not 'behold'.
נָא, a particle of entreaty.
לִ with the 1st singular suffix; with the numeral, 'I have'.
relative particle.
negative of the verb: 'never' in English.
qatal, 3rd plural common, with the daughters as subject. 'Know a man' is the biblical euphemism for sexual relations.
hifil cohortative, 1st singular: 'let me bring out'.
נָא again, after the verb.
the object marker with the 3rd feminine plural suffix.
imperative with the conjunction: 'and do'.
כְּ 'as' with the article and the adjective טוֹב: 'as the good (thing) in your eyes'; the pack reads it as sense 5 'good, appropriate, becoming'. In English: 'as you see fit'.
'in your eyes': in your judgment.
הָאֵל is 'these' (אֵלֶּה, shorter form); see the Ibn Ezra comment.
the negative of the jussive.
jussive, 2nd plural: 'do not'.
דָבָר as 'matter, affair', with the negative: 'nothing'.
כִּי עַל כֵּן is one conjunction, 'forasmuch as': the three words are a unit.
qatal, 3rd plural: 'they came in'.
בְּצֵל, 'in the shadow of'.
קֹרָה is a beam or rafter of the house; here it stands for the house roof.

phrases.english: Look, please, I have two daughters
phrases.literal: 'look-please to-me two daughters': the interjections open the speech; 'to me' with the numeral is 'I have'.

phrases.english: who have never known a man
phrases.literal: 'who not knew man': the negative goes with the verb, so 'never'; 'have known' keeps the euphemism.

phrases.english: Let me bring them out to you now
phrases.literal: 'let-me-bring-out now them to-you': the cohortative first, then the particle 'now'; 'them' is the object marker with its suffix.

phrases.english: and do to them as you see fit
phrases.literal: 'and-do to-them as-good in-eyes-of-you': 'as good in your eyes' is the Hebrew idiom for 'as you see fit'.

phrases.english: Only to these men
phrases.literal: 'only to-the-men these': the particle comes first; 'these' follows the noun.

phrases.english: do not do anything
phrases.literal: 'not do a-thing': the jussive negative אַל with the noun 'a thing'; 'nothing' would read as 'do nothing at all'

phrases.english: since
phrases.literal: 'for-on-account-of-this': one conjunction, 'forasmuch as'; Rashi and Radak read it as 'because they came under my roof'

phrases.english: they have come under the shelter of my roof
phrases.literal: 'came in-shadow-of roof-of-me': the completed act of coming in, under the protection of the host's house.

grammar: הִנֵּה and נָא open Lot's speech to the men of Sodom: an interjection and an entreaty, 'look' and 'please'. The whole verse is direct speech, so it is set in double quotation marks.

יָדְעוּ is a qatal, 3rd plural, with the daughters as subject, and the negative לֹא belongs to it. The verb has the lexicon sense 'know a person', the biblical euphemism for sexual relations. Ibn Ezra notes that the one form serves masculine and feminine plural.

אוֹצִיאָה is a cohortative (hifil, 1st singular, 'let me bring out'); the particle נָא comes after it, so the offer is softened by the cohortative and again by נָא. The imperative וַעֲשׂוּ then gives the crowd leave to act.
הָאֵל is a short form of הָאֵלֶּה, 'these', and follows its noun: 'the men these' (Ibn Ezra, Rashi).
כִּי עַל כֵּן (the lexicon: 'forasmuch as') gives the ground of Lot's plea: the men have come under his roof, so they are not to be harmed. Rashi and Radak read it 'because they came'.

The pashta on יָדְעוּ is a minor pause; the zaqef qaton on אִישׁ closes the relative clause, the etnaḥta on בְּעֵינֵיכֶם divides the offer from the protection of the guests, and the silluq on קֹרָתִי ends the verse.
segments.note: Lot's offer to the crowd is the plain sense of the verse: his daughters in place of his guests. The English keeps the offer as Lot makes it and does not comment on it; the commentators (Ramban, Sforno) discuss his motive.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra says יָדְעוּ is the plural of the past tense used of masculine and feminine alike, with no added vav and the same vowel in both. The English takes the verb with the two daughters as its subject.

Ibn Ezra: הָאֵל is the same as הָאֵלֶּה, 'these'. The Gaon said it was written so because of the third man who had not come; Ibn Ezra calls that reason remote, since both forms, the short and the long, are found in Aramaic. The English 'these' follows him.
Rashi, like Ibn Ezra, reads הָאֵל as כְּמוֹ הָאֵלֶּה, 'these'.
Rashi paraphrases the clause as 'you will do this good for my honour, because they came under the shelter of my roof'. The English keeps the causal link and does not add the honour.

apparatus: הָאֵל (19:8.20) is read as 'these' (הָאֵלֶּה) by Ibn Ezra and Rashi. Ibn Ezra reports the Gaon's reason for the short form, 'because of the third (man) who did not come', and rejects it as remote, since both forms occur in Aramaic.
context: The shelter of the roof-beam (קֹרָה) names the host's protection of a guest who has come under his roof; Lot's plea rests on that duty.
Offering one's daughters to a crowd in place of guests recurs in Judges 19:24, where a host makes the same offer; Ramban compares the two cases.

segments.english: And they said, "Get out of the way!" And they said, "This one came to sojourn, and he has set himself up as a judge. Now we will treat you worse than them." And they pressed upon the man, upon Lot, very hard; and they drew near to break the door.
segments.literal: and-said they draw-near further-on and-said they the-one came to-sojourn and-judged judging now we-do-harm to-you more-than-them and-pressed they on-the-man on-Lot exceedingly and-drew-near they to-break the-door

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of amar, 3rd plural: the narrative sequence.
imperative of nagash, 'draw near'; in this idiom it is a command to move off.
the adverb הָלְאָה, 'further, out there', with the directional ending.
second wayyiqtol; it introduces the second speech.
the article with the numeral 'one': 'this one'.
qatal, 3rd masculine singular.
infinitive construct with the prefix lamed: 'to sojourn', to live as a resident alien.
wayyiqtol of shafat: 'and he acted as judge'.
infinitive absolute beside the wayyiqtol: it stresses the verb.
hifil imperfect, 1st plural: 'we will do harm'.
מִן with the 3rd plural suffix, the comparative 'than'.
wayyiqtol of patsar: 'press hard'.
wayyiqtol of nagash: 'they came up close'.
infinitive construct of shavar, 'break'.

phrases.english: And they said, Get out of the way
phrases.literal: 'and-said they; get-away; there-further': a command, not a request.

phrases.english: and they said, This one came to sojourn, and he has set himself up as a judge
phrases.literal: 'and-said they; the-one came to-sojourn; and-judged judging': the infinitive absolute adds emphasis to the self-appointed judging.

phrases.english: Now we will treat you worse than them
phrases.literal: 'now do-harm to-you from-them': the threat is that the men will do Lot more harm than they do the guests.

phrases.english: and they pressed upon the man, upon Lot, very hard
phrases.literal: 'and-pressed they on-the-man on-Lot exceedingly': the repeated preposition marks the force of the pressure.

phrases.english: and they drew near to break the door
phrases.literal: 'and-drew-near they to-break the-door': the purpose of the approach is the breaking of the door.

grammar: The two וַיֹּאמְרוּ (wayyiqtol, 3rd plural) open two separate speeches of the crowd. The wayyiqtols וַיִּפְצְרוּ and וַיִּגְּשׁוּ then carry the narrative; וַיִּשְׁפֹּט is inside the speech, 'and he has acted as judge'.

The first speech is one command: גֶּשׁ is the imperative of נָגַשׁ, 'draw near', with הָלְאָה, 'further on'. The two together mean 'move on, stand back' (Rashi: draw aside and keep away; Radak: go to another place). Ramban finds the clue in the verb that follows.
הָאֶחָד has the article: 'the one', 'this one fellow', said with contempt. The word order puts him first and the verbs follow.
The infinitive absolute שָׁפוֹט beside the wayyiqtol וַיִּשְׁפֹּט stresses the verb: 'and he would play the judge'.
נָרַע is a hifil imperfect, 1st plural, 'we will do harm'; לְךָ is the one harmed and מֵהֶם is the comparative 'than (to) them'.
segments.note: The Hebrew says only 'the man' and 'Lot'; the English keeps the name and the phrase 'upon the man, upon Lot' as the repetition of the preposition has it.

commentary.summary: Rashi glosses גֶּשׁ הָלְאָה as 'move aside and keep away from him', and calls it a rebuke: 'we are not concerned about you'.

Ramban: he finds the verb פצר only in words of appeasement (פִּיּוּסִים). So either the men begged Lot to open the door to them and, when he refused, came near to break him (לִשְׁבֹּר אוֹתוֹ), or Lot stood before the door and they begged him to step aside, because they did not want to hurt him; that is the sense of 'גֶּשׁ הָלְאָה', that he move to another place. The English keeps 'pressed' and does not decide between the two.

context: גּוּר, 'sojourn', is the status of a resident alien: a man who settles outside his own kin among strangers, under the protection of the local people but without a native's standing. The crowd's charge is that such a newcomer presumes to judge them; Lot is said to have settled in Sodom in 13:12.

segments.english: And the men stretched out their hands, and brought Lot to them, into the house, and shut the door.
segments.literal: and-stretched-out the-men (object) their-hand and-brought-in (object) Lot to-them housewards and-(object) the-door shut

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of shalah in the sense 'stretch out': the men reach out the hand to pull Lot in. (Here without בְּ, so not 'lay hands on'.)
יָד is singular with a plural suffix, 'their hand'; the English line uses the plural, as English does with this idiom.
hifil wayyiqtol of bo': 'and they caused to come in'.
the directional ending of בַּיִת: 'housewards, inwards'.
conjunction with the object marker.
qatal, 3rd plural: 'they shut'.

phrases.english: And the men stretched out their hands
phrases.literal: 'and-stretched-out the-men (object) their-hand': they reach out to pull Lot in; the noun is singular.

phrases.english: and brought Lot to them, into the house
phrases.literal: 'and-brought-in (object) Lot to-them housewards': the directional ending gives 'into the house'.

phrases.english: and shut the door
phrases.literal: 'and the-door shut': the door is set first in the Hebrew.

grammar: The two wayyiqtols וַיִּשְׁלְחוּ and וַיָּבִיאוּ carry the narrative; the third verb, סָגָרוּ, is a qatal with its object set first: 'and the door they shut', a closing act that goes with the bringing in.
הַבָּיְתָה is the directional form of בַּיִת; the ending marks motion, 'into the house'.
The etnaḥta on הַבָּיְתָה divides the verse; the tipḥa on אֲלֵיהֶם only separates the words within the second clause.
The verse ends with the silluq on סָגָרוּ.
segments.note: The men who took Lot in are the two visitors of verse 1; the text calls them 'men' here and does not name them.

commentary.summary: Onkelos renders שָׁלְחוּ יָדָם as 'they extended their hands', the same reading as 'stretched out their hands'.

segments.english: And the men who were at the entrance of the house they struck with blindness, from the least to the greatest; and they wore themselves out searching for the entrance.
segments.literal: and-the-men who at-entrance-of the-house they-struck with-blindness from-small to-great and-they-wore-out to-find the-entrance

tokens.note: conjunction with the object marker.
relative particle.
פֶּתַח in the construct before 'the house'.
hifil qatal, 3rd plural: 'smite, strike'.
סַנְוֵרִים, a sudden blindness or dazzling; see the Ibn Ezra comment.
מִן with the adjective 'small'.
עַד, 'up to, as far as', of degree.
'great' in importance: the fixed pair 'from small to great' means all of them.
wayyiqtol of la'ah, 'be weary': 'they tired themselves out'.
infinitive construct of matsa' with the prefix lamed.

phrases.english: And the men who were at the entrance of the house
phrases.literal: 'and-the-men who at-entrance-of the-house': the subject is set first, before the verb.

phrases.english: they struck with blindness, from the least to the greatest
phrases.literal: 'they-struck with-blindness from-small to-great': a fixed pair, 'all of them'.

phrases.english: and they wore themselves out searching for the entrance
phrases.literal: 'and-they-wore-out to-find the-entrance': the weariness is the result of the search.

grammar: The subject of הִכּוּ is the two visitors; the men struck are the men of Sodom 'at the entrance of the house'. The object is set first, with the particle אֶת, before the verb.
The pair מִקָּטֹן וְעַד־גָּדוֹל, 'from small to great', is a fixed phrase for all of the people, of every age and rank.
The wayyiqtol וַיִּלְאוּ continues the sequence, and its infinitive לִמְצֹא states what they wearied themselves over: they could not find the entrance.
The verse ends with the silluq on הַפָּתַח; the entrance is named twice, first as a place and then as the thing sought.
segments.note: סַנְוֵרִים is rare; the English 'blindness' follows the lexicon and Rashi. Ibn Ezra's 'darkening of the eye and of the heart' is recorded in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: a rare word (he calls it מלה רביעית), whose companion is in the story of Elisha (2 Kings 6:18); its meaning is a darkening of the eye and of the heart. The English 'blindness' carries the eye; the 'heart' (a clouding of the mind) is not in the English and is recorded here.
Rashi glosses בַּסַּנְוֵרִים as מַכַּת עִוָּרוֹן, a plague of blindness.

Rashi's midrash reads 'from small to great' as the young beginning the sin, so that the plague began with them. This is midrash, not the plain sense; the English keeps 'from the least to the greatest'.

apparatus: סַנְוֵרִים (19:11.7) is rare, found also in 2 Kings 6:18; the English follows the lexicon's 'sudden blindness'.

segments.english: And the men said to Lot, "If you have anyone else here, a son-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and all that you have in the city, bring them out of this place.
segments.literal: and-said the-men to-Lot still who to-you here a-son-in-law and-your-sons and-your-daughters and-all which to-you in-the-city bring-out from the-place

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of amar, 3rd plural.
עוֹד: 'still, further, else'. Ibn Ezra paraphrases the question as a condition, 'if you have ...'; the English line carries the condition in 'If you have anyone else'.
interrogative מִי used as 'anyone'.
לְ with the 2nd masculine singular suffix: 'to you', 'you have'.

בָּנֶיךָ is 'your sons'. Ibn Ezra takes it as 'sons-in-law who are as your sons and daughters'; Rashi and Radak, 'the sons of your married daughters' (Lot has no sons). The English keeps 'sons' and records the rest.
relative particle.
hifil imperative, 2nd masculine singular: the object 'them' is understood.
מִן with a verb of removal: 'out of'.

phrases.english: And the men said to Lot
phrases.literal: 'and-said the-men to-Lot'.

phrases.english: If you have anyone else here
phrases.literal: 'still who to-you here': the question is read as a condition, 'if there is anyone of yours here'.

phrases.english: a son-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and all that you have in the city
phrases.literal: 'a-son-in-law and-your-sons and-your-daughters and-all which to-you in-the-city': the relatives in order, then all the possessions

phrases.english: bring them out of this place
phrases.literal: 'bring-out from the-place': the imperative; 'them' is supplied from the list.

grammar: עוֹד מִי לְךָ פֹּה is an idiom: literally 'still who to you here', 'who else do you have here'. Rashi (his plain sense) and Radak take it as a question; Ibn Ezra paraphrases it as a condition, 'if you have a son-in-law', and the English follows him.

The list runs חָתָן (singular), בָּנֶיךָ, בְּנֹתֶיךָ (plural), then כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־לְךָ בָּעִיר, 'all that is yours in the city'. It stands before the verb as one long object, and הוֹצֵא then governs the whole list.
הוֹצֵא is a hifil imperative, 2nd masculine singular, addressed to Lot; the object is the list before it.
The etnaḥta on בָּעִיר divides the list from the command; the silluq on הַמָּקוֹם ends the verse.
segments.note: The English reads the condition (Ibn Ezra) and keeps 'your sons' as the Hebrew has it. Ibn Ezra's 'sons-in-law who are as sons' and the reading of Rashi and Radak, 'the sons of your married daughters' (Lot has no sons), are recorded in the apparatus and the commentary.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra paraphrases the phrase as 'if you have a son-in-law', so he takes the question as a condition. The English 'If you have anyone else here' keeps that reading.

Ibn Ezra: ובניך is 'or sons-in-law who are as your sons and your daughters'. He adds that this verse is an argument against those who say that one (angel) went to save Lot: both spoke to Lot (v. 12), and also say 'for we are destroying' (v. 13), and the one with whom Lot spoke afterwards, who answered 'you have magnified your kindness' (v. 19), said 'for I cannot do anything' (v. 22). The English keeps 'your sons' and records his reading.
Rashi takes ובניך as the sons of the married daughters, and Radak says the same since Lot had no sons. The English keeps 'your sons-in-law' from Ibn Ezra and records this reading.

apparatus: ובניך (19:12.10) is 'your sons'. Ibn Ezra reads 'sons-in-law who are as your sons and daughters'; Rashi and Radak, 'the sons of your married daughters', since Lot had no sons (Radak). The English keeps 'your sons', the plain word.

segments.english: For we are about to destroy this place, because their outcry has grown great before the LORD, and the LORD sent us to destroy it."
segments.literal: for destroying we the-place this for has-grown-great their-outcry before the-presence-of the-LORD and-sent-us the-LORD to-destroy-it

tokens.note: כִּי introducing a causal clause.
hifil participle, masculine plural, used of an action about to happen: 'we are about to destroy'.
the independent pronoun of the speakers.
the second causal כִּי: the reason for the destruction.
qatal, 3rd feminine singular, agreeing with צַעֲקָה.
the suffix is the object of the cry: the outcry against them.
אֵת פְּנֵי, 'before the presence of', the lexicon's special use.
YHWH, rendered LORD in capitals.
piel wayyiqtol of shalah with the 1st plural suffix: 'and he sent us'.
piel infinitive construct of shahat with the 3rd feminine singular suffix; the suffix refers to the city of verse 12 (עִיר, feminine), which Radak says is included in 'the place'.

phrases.english: For we are about to destroy this place
phrases.literal: 'for destroying we (object) the-place this': the speakers' own intended act.

phrases.english: because their outcry has grown great before the LORD
phrases.literal: 'for has-grown-great their-outcry before the-presence-of the-LORD': the outcry reaches the LORD.

phrases.english: and the LORD sent us to destroy it
phrases.literal: 'and-sent-us the-LORD to-destroy-it': the LORD is the one who sent the men.

grammar: כִּי opens two causal clauses: 'for we are about to destroy' and 'for their outcry has grown great'.
The participle מַשְׁחִתִים is a hifil, with the speakers as subject; the participle with the pronoun states an action under way or about to begin.
גָּדְלָה is a qatal with the feminine subject צַעֲקָתָם, and the verb agrees with its subject.
The verse ends with the silluq on לְשַׁחֲתָהּ; the feminine suffix refers to the city (עִיר, v. 12), not to the masculine מָקוֹם; Radak says the city is included in 'the place'.
segments.note: The English keeps 'their outcry' as the Hebrew has it; Radak's reading (the cry of the oppressed against them) fits the same words and is recorded.

commentary.summary: Radak says 'their outcry' is the cry of the oppressed who call out against those people, the suffix being the object of the cry. The English keeps the literal words, which cover this reading.

context: צְעָקָה, 'outcry', is the cry of the wronged appealing for redress; in 18:20–21 the same kind of outcry from Sodom and Gomorrah is what brings the LORD to look into the cities.

segments.english: And Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, who had married his daughters, and said, "Get up, get out of this place, for the LORD is destroying the city." But to his sons-in-law he seemed like a man joking.
segments.literal: and-went-out Lot and-spoke to-sons-in-law-of-him takers-of daughters-of-him and-said get-up go-out from-the-place this for destroying the-LORD the-city and-was as-one-joking in-eyes-of sons-in-law-of-him

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of yatsa', 'go out from a place'.
piel wayyiqtol of dabar.

participle construct of laqah, 'takers of', i.e. men who take (took) daughters of his as wives. The participle has no tense of its own: Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as already done; Rashi adds that the two at home were betrothed.
wayyiqtol of amar.
imperative of qum, plural.
imperative of yatsa', plural.
כִּי introducing the reason.
hifil participle, masculine singular: 'is destroying'.
wayyiqtol of hayah: 'he became, seemed'.
כְּ with the piel participle of tsahaq: 'like one jesting'.

phrases.english: And Lot went out
phrases.literal: 'and-went-out Lot'.

phrases.english: and spoke to his sons-in-law, who had married his daughters
phrases.literal: 'and-spoke to-sons-in-law-of-him takers-of daughters-of-him': the participle has no tense of its own; Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as already done

phrases.english: and said
phrases.literal: 'and-said': the speech follows.

phrases.english: Get up, get out of this place
phrases.literal: 'get-up go-out from-the-place this': two plural imperatives.

phrases.english: for the LORD is destroying the city
phrases.literal: 'for destroying the-LORD (object) the-city': the reason for the command.

phrases.english: to his sons-in-law he seemed like a man joking
phrases.literal: 'and-was as-one-joking in-eyes-of sons-in-law-of-him': the narrator's comment on their reaction.

grammar: וַיֵּצֵא, וַיְדַבֵּר, and וַיֹּאמֶר are wayyiqtols: Lot goes out, speaks, and says; וַיְהִי then carries the narrator's comment.

לֹקְחֵי בְנֹתָיו is a participle in the construct plural, 'takers of his daughters'. A participle has no tense of its own: 'who had married' follows Ibn Ezra and Radak (already taken); Rashi's betrothal reading would be 'who were to take'.
קוּמוּ and צְּאוּ are two plural imperatives addressed to the sons-in-law; the reason follows in a clause with the participle מַשְׁחִית.
וַיְהִי כִמְצַחֵק: 'he was like one jesting' (piel participle of צָחַק, BDB 'jest'), 'in the eyes of' his sons-in-law, that is, in their view.
The etnaḥta on הָעִיר ends Lot's words and the narrator's line follows; the silluq on חֲתָנָיו closes the verse.
segments.note: The English says only 'his daughters' and does not say which daughters; Ibn Ezra holds that Lot had two other daughters, who died in Sodom, besides the two of verse 15; Rashi adds a betrothal reading for the two at home. The English follows Ibn Ezra and Radak that the men had already married.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: Lot had two other daughters, and they died in Sodom; the proof (הָעֵד) is the word הַנִּמְצָאֹת in the next verse, 'the ones found' (at home), which implies others who were not. So the 'takers of his daughters' are the husbands of those other daughters, already married. The English 'who had married his daughters' agrees; the comment is brief and this last step is its sense.
Rashi: Lot had two married daughters in the city, so the 'sons-in-law' are their husbands. The English 'who had married his daughters' agrees.
Rashi on 'takers of his daughters': those (daughters) at home were betrothed to them. The English does not adopt this; it is recorded here and in the apparatus.

Radak: the sons-in-law had already taken Lot's daughters (שֶׁלְּקָחוּם כְּבָר); the text does not say that Lot spoke to his daughters because wives follow the judgment of their husbands. The English 'who had married' gives the same.

apparatus: לֹקְחֵי בְנֹתָיו (19:14.6–7): Ibn Ezra and Radak take the men as already married to daughters of Lot; Ibn Ezra adds that these were two daughters other than the two found at home (v. 15). Rashi also has the two at home betrothed to them. The English 'had married' follows the first.
context: A betrothed woman was treated in law as already married (Deuteronomy 22:23-24). The 'takers' of this verse may be men with a betrothal, so the status of the daughters is a question for the commentators.

segments.english: As the dawn rose, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Get up, take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the guilt of the city."
segments.literal: and-as the-dawn rose and-urged the-angels in-Lot saying rise take (object) your-wife and-(object) two-of your-daughters the-ones-found lest be-swept-away in-iniquity-of the-city

tokens.note: conjunction with כְּמוֹ, 'as' or 'when'.
qatal, 3rd masculine singular: 'go up, rise'.
hifil wayyiqtol of 'uts: 'press, hurry'. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'pressed'.
מַלְאָךְ as 'angel', a being sent by God.
בְּ with the name: 'upon Lot'.
infinitive construct of amar introducing the speech.
imperative, 2nd masculine singular.
imperative of laqah: 'take and carry along'.
conjunction with the object marker.
nifal participle, feminine plural, of matsa': 'found'. Radak: 'with you in the house'.
פֶּן with the imperfect: 'lest'.
nifal imperfect, 2nd masculine singular: 'be swept away, destroyed'.
בַּ with עָוֹן, 'iniquity, guilt'.

phrases.english: As the dawn rose
phrases.literal: 'and-as the-dawn rose': the clause gives the time; see Ibn Ezra.

phrases.english: the angels urged Lot, saying
phrases.literal: 'urged the-angels upon-Lot saying': the men urged him, as the wayyiqtol's pressure suggests.

phrases.english: Get up, take your wife
phrases.literal: 'get-up take (object) your-wife': two imperatives.

phrases.english: and your two daughters who are here
phrases.literal: 'and (object) two your-daughters who-are-found': the participle is 'those found here'.

phrases.english: lest you be swept away in the guilt of the city
phrases.literal: 'lest be-swept-away in-guilt-of the-city': the purpose of the command.

grammar: וּכְמוֹ הַשַּׁחַר עָלָה is a clause of time: 'and as the dawn rose'. Ibn Ezra defends the construction against R. Jonah's objection.
The wayyiqtol וַיָּאִיצוּ, with the subject the angels, introduces the speech with the infinitive לֵאמֹר, 'saying'.
קוּם and קַח are two imperatives; the two objects, 'your wife' and 'your two daughters', are the people to be taken out.

The participle הַנִּמְצָאֹת is nifal, feminine plural, agreeing with 'your daughters': 'who are found, who are here'. Ibn Ezra's reading of the previous verse takes it to imply other daughters who were not there.
The verse ends with the silluq on הָעִיר; the lest-clause (פֶּן with the imperfect) gives the danger.
segments.note: The angels are called 'the men' in verses 10-12 and 'the angels' here; the verse marks the change. The English follows the Hebrew noun and keeps 'urged' for the verb.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra quotes R. Jonah the grammarian, who held that 'and as the dawn rose' cannot be said, and says that Jonah forgot 'they multiplied as they multiplied' (Zechariah 10:8), where the same construction occurs. The English reads the clause as 'as the dawn rose'.
Ibn Ezra glosses וַיָּאִיצוּ as ויציקו, 'they pressed', comparing the word in Exodus 5:13, where the taskmasters press the people. The English 'urged' keeps that pressure.
Radak takes הַנִּמְצָאֹת as 'those found with you in the house'. The English 'who are here' gives the same sense.
Rashi reads הַנִּמְצָאֹת as 'those prepared for you in the house, to save them'. The English keeps 'who are here' and records his reading.
